kurals.tamil:
பழைமை எனப்படுவது யாதெனின் யாதும்
கிழமையைக் கீழ்ந்திடா நட்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Pazhaimai enappaduvadhu yaadhenin yaadhum
kizhamaiyaik keezhndhidaa natpu.
kurals.meaning: If you ask what ‘long-standing friendship’ really is, it is the friendship that never slights, in any way, the liberties an old friend takes because of that closeness.
kurals.elementary: A brand-new classmate has to knock before borrowing your pencil. Your oldest friend just picks it up, and you don’t mind at all. That not-minding is what a really old friendship looks like.
kurals.university: The chapter opens with a definition. Pazhaimai (பழைமை, ‘oldness’) is the friendship that has grown old, and kizhamai (கிழமை) is the ‘right’ or ‘claim’ (urimai, உரிமை) that such long intimacy creates; keezhndhidaa (கீழ்ந்திடா) means ‘does not cut down, belittle or set aside’. Read with yaadhum (‘in anything at all’), the couplet says that true old friendship never treats the friend’s presumptions as offences. Parimelazhagar places the chapter directly after Natpaaraaydhal (testing a friend before befriending) and the commentarial tradition reads it as the next stage: once a friend has been tested and kept, the bond should bear the freedoms that time brings. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss the couplet as accepting what the old friend does by right of intimacy, while Puliyur Kesigan reads it more broadly as a friendship that lets nothing damage the established bond. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As a father tolerates his son, a friend forgives his friend, and a lover pardons the beloved, please forgive me for my offences.”
hinduism.explanation: After seeing Krishna’s cosmic form, Arjuna asks to be forgiven for years of easy familiarity, appealing to the forbearance a friend naturally shows a friend.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita takes for granted exactly what the Kural defines: a true friend does not hold the liberties of intimacy against the other.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match on forbearance between friends, though the setting is devotional rather than a teaching on friendship.

christianity.quote_or_event: Ben Sira advises his student not to forsake an old friend, because a new friend cannot compare with him: a new friend is like new wine, which is enjoyed best once it has aged.
christianity.explanation: Sirach ranks the long-tested friend above any newcomer and compares maturing friendship to wine that improves with age. Sirach is deuterocanonical, part of Catholic and Orthodox Scripture but not the Protestant canon.
christianity.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Ben Sira gives the old friend a standing that a new acquaintance cannot claim.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close in theme, but paraphrased because the wording could not be checked against a live source this session.

islam.quote_or_event: “the Prophet (ﷺ) used to mention her very often, and when ever he slaughtered a sheep, he would cut its parts and send them to the women friends of Khadija.”
islam.explanation: Aisha recalls that, years after Khadija died, the Prophet kept honouring the friends of his first wife.
islam.tie_back: This shows the faithfulness to old ties that the Kural calls pazhaimai, kept up long after the relationship began.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the honouring of old bonds, but it concerns a late wife’s friends rather than tolerance of a friend’s liberties.

judaism.quote_or_event: “All love that depends on a something, [when the] thing ceases, [the] love ceases; and [all love] that does not depend on anything, will never cease. … And what is an example of love that did not depend on anything? Such was the love of David and Jonathan.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah says that love which depends on some benefit ends when the benefit ends, but love that depends on nothing lasts forever, as David and Jonathan’s did.
judaism.tie_back: Love that ‘depends on nothing’ does not keep accounts of slights, so it fits Valluvar’s definition of a friendship that nothing diminishes.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 5:16 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on durable, unconditional friendship; the specific idea of accepting liberties is implied rather than stated.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He gives what is hard to give. He does what is hard to do. He endures what is hard to endure.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists qualities that make a friend worth keeping, starting with generosity, effort and endurance on the friend’s behalf.
buddhism.tie_back: Enduring what is hard to endure includes putting up with what an intimate friend does, which is the forbearance the Kural describes.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.35, Mitta Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: General portrait of a true friend; it does not speak specifically of old friendship or its liberties.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus comes home in disguise after twenty years, his old hound Argos, neglected and lying on a dung heap, recognizes him at once, wags his tail and drops his ears, and then dies.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer gives the first recognition of the returning hero to an old companion whose attachment twenty years of absence had not worn away.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Argos is a picture of the bond the Kural praises, one that time and changed circumstances do not reduce.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Loose analogy: a story of loyalty between a man and a dog, not a teaching about friends’ liberties.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The older the sweeter, as in wines that keep well. And the proverb is a true one, "You must eat many a peck of salt with a man to be thorough friends with him."”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius argues that, other things being equal, old friendships should be preferred to new ones, since friendship grows richer with age.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero and Valluvar agree that time is what gives friendship its value and its rights.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 19 (§67), trans. E. S. Shuckburgh
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the chapter’s praise of old friendship; the Kural’s specific point about tolerating liberties is not stated here.

kurals.tamil:
நட்பிற் குறுப்புக் கெழுதகைமை மற்றதற்கு
உப்பாதல் சான்றோர் கடன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Natpir kuruppuk kezhudhakaimai matradharku
uppaadhal saandror kadan.
kurals.meaning: The freedoms friends take with each other are part of what friendship is made of, and it is the duty of good people to welcome those freedoms and enjoy them.
kurals.elementary: Salt makes food taste right. In a friendship, the little freedoms friends take, like finishing your sentences or grabbing a fry off your plate, are the salt. A good person does not complain about the salt; they enjoy the meal.
kurals.university: Uruppu (உறுப்பு, ‘limb, constituent part’) makes kezhudhakaimai (கெழுதகைமை, ‘the quality of intimate right’) a structural part of friendship, not an extra. The second line turns on uppu (உப்பு, ‘salt’), which the commentators read figuratively as relish or sweetness: the wise should be the salt to that intimacy, accepting it and taking pleasure in it. Mu. Varadarasanar reads uppaadhal as ‘agreeing to’ the friend’s act of right, Solomon Pappaiah as ‘rejoicing at it’, and Puliyur Kesigan as ‘acting as the very model of that intimacy’. G. U. Pope’s ‘to be its savour sweet is duty of the wise’ keeps the image of salt. Saandror (சான்றோர்) are the cultivated people whose kadan (கடன், ‘duty, obligation’) this is. Both base sources give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the poor Brahmin Sudama visits his childhood friend Krishna, now a king, he is too ashamed to offer the handful of flattened rice he has brought. Krishna pulls the bundle from him himself and eats it with delight.
hinduism.explanation: In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna takes an old friend’s liberty, grabbing a gift that was not offered, and treats the humble rice as a treasure.
hinduism.tie_back: The episode shows familiarity working as the ‘salt’ of friendship: freedom taken and freedom received with joy on both sides.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good narrative illustration of intimate freedom between old friends; paraphrased, not quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus tells his disciples that he no longer calls them servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing, but calls them friends, because he has made known to them everything he heard from the Father.
christianity.explanation: The relationship moves from formal service to the openness of friendship, defined by shared confidence.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, intimacy and its freedoms are what separate friendship from a mere formal tie.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the idea that intimacy defines friendship, but says nothing about welcoming a friend’s liberties.

islam.quote_or_event: After the emigration to Medina, the Prophet paired emigrants with Medinan helpers as brothers. Sa‘d ibn al-Rabi‘ offered his new brother ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf half of his property; ‘Abd al-Rahman thanked him, declined, and asked only to be shown the market.
islam.explanation: The early brotherhood (mu’akhat) was a bond of such familiarity that each could claim from the other what strangers could not.
islam.tie_back: Islamic tradition treats such claims between bonded friends as natural and generous, which is the urimai the Kural calls part of friendship itself.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Merits of the Helpers (Ansar), report of Sa‘d ibn al-Rabi‘ and ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf
islam._accuracy_note: Illustrates rights between bonded companions; paraphrased from memory without a verified hadith number.

judaism.quote_or_event: “appoint for thyself a teacher, and acquire for thyself a companion and judge all men with the scale weighted in his favor.”
judaism.explanation: Joshua ben Perahiah tells each person to make the effort to gain a companion and to read others’ actions charitably.
judaism.tie_back: Gaining a companion and judging generously together come close to the Kural’s view that taking friends’ freedoms in good part is a duty.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:6 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Partial match: the duty to keep a companion and judge favourably, not a direct statement about intimate liberties.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the advice to Sigala, the Buddha says a lay follower should treat friends with generosity, kind speech, helpfulness, impartiality and sincerity, and lists among the marks of a true friend one who is the same in happiness and in sorrow.
buddhism.explanation: Friendship is described as a set of mutual, reciprocal duties.
buddhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar, the Buddha makes friendship a duty for good people, not just a pleasure.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Broadly parallel on the duties of friendship; nothing specific about liberties of intimacy.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles and Patroclus grew up together in Peleus’ house and share a tent, food and armour at Troy; Patroclus’ ghost asks that their bones lie together in one urn.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Iliad presents their companionship as shared life and shared possessions, built up from childhood.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Their total familiarity, with nothing held back, is the kind of bond in which the Kural says liberties are part of friendship.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates deep familiarity but not the ethic of accepting a friend’s presumptions.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “to comrades and brothers one should allow freedom of speech and common use of all things.”
philosophy.explanation: Discussing what is owed to different kinds of people, Aristotle says close companions are owed frankness and shared use of possessions.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly Valluvar’s point: the freedoms of intimacy belong to friendship, and allowing them is a duty.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.2 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close match: intimate liberty as something owed to close friends.

kurals.tamil:
பழகிய நட்பெவன் செய்யுங் கெழுதகைமை
செய்தாங்கு அமையாக் கடை.
kurals.transliteration:
Pazhakiya natpevan seyyung kezhudhakaimai
seydhaangu amaiyaak kadai.
kurals.meaning: What good is a friendship kept up for years if you won’t accept what your friend does by right of that closeness as though you had done it yourself?
kurals.elementary: Imagine your best friend signs both your names on a birthday card for your teacher without asking. If you get cross, what was all that friendship for? A real friend says, ‘Good idea, that’s what I would have done.’
kurals.university: The couplet is a rhetorical question: evan seyyum (எவன் செய்யும், ‘what will it do?’) asks what use a long-practised friendship (pazhakiya natpu) has if one does not seydhaangu amaidhal (செய்தாங்கு அமைதல்), ‘acquiesce as though one had done it oneself’, in what the friend did by kezhudhakaimai (intimate right). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take this as owning the friend’s act; Solomon Pappaiah adds that this holds even when one does not personally agree with it. Puliyur Kesigan reads the line from the other side: if the same intimacy is not present in the friend too, the long acquaintance is useless. That reading shows the couplet can be taken as a statement about reciprocity. The text is the same in both base sources (with the sandhi form seyyung).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And if, jestfully, I treated You with disrespect, while playing, resting, sitting, eating, when alone, or before others—for all that I crave forgiveness.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna remembers years of casual companionship with Krishna, joking, eating and resting together, and Krishna never took offence.
hinduism.tie_back: Krishna accepted his friend’s familiar behaviour without complaint, which is the acceptance the Kural says gives an old friendship its value.
hinduism._accuracy_note: The verse shows the familiarity and implies Krishna’s acceptance; it is Arjuna’s apology, not a rule about friends.

christianity.quote_or_event: Writing to his friend Philemon, Paul sends back the runaway Onesimus, now a Christian, and asks Philemon to receive him as he would receive Paul himself, offering to repay any debt and noting that Philemon owes Paul his own self.
christianity.explanation: Paul uses the freedom of an old friendship to ask a great deal and trusts Philemon to treat the request as his own.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ideal in practice: a friend’s act of familiarity received as if one had done it oneself.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good illustration of a request made on the strength of friendship; Paul asks rather than acting first.

islam.quote_or_event: When Abu Bakr and ‘Umar fell out, the Prophet told those present not to leave his companion exposed to blame, reminding them that Abu Bakr had believed in him when others called him a liar.
islam.explanation: The Prophet defended the standing of a long-standing companion against criticism of his conduct.
islam.tie_back: He treated an old friend’s place as his own concern, which is close to the Kural’s ideal of owning a friend’s acts.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Companions, narration of Abu al-Darda’
islam._accuracy_note: Loyalty to an old companion; paraphrased from memory without a verified hadith number.

judaism.quote_or_event: On the day David kills Goliath, Jonathan’s soul is bound to David’s. Jonathan makes a covenant with him and, without being asked, gives David his own robe, armour, sword, bow and belt.
judaism.explanation: The prince hands over the symbols of his rank to the friend he loves.
judaism.tie_back: Jonathan treats what is his as David’s, the complete identification of interests the Kural asks of old friends.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shows friends’ interests fully merged; the Kural’s case of accepting a friend’s act afterwards is not directly addressed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He reveals his secrets to you. He keeps your secrets.”
buddhism.explanation: Among the marks of a friend worth keeping, the Buddha lists mutual confidence: sharing secrets and guarding the other’s.
buddhism.tie_back: That kind of mutual trust is what lets a friend act for you and have it accepted as your own act.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.35, Mitta Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Related through trust and intimacy, not through accepting a friend’s acts.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides’ Iphigenia among the Taurians, Orestes and Pylades each insist on dying in the other’s place, and each treats the other’s fate as his own.
greek_mythology.explanation: The two cousins and companions are so close that neither will accept survival at the other’s cost.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Their friendship makes no distinction between ‘his act’ and ‘mine’, which is the identification the Kural requires.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates friends sharing one fate; it is a story of self-sacrifice, not of accepting a friend’s liberties.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Every one likes ceteris paribus to use the horse to which he has been accustomed, rather than one that is untried and new.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero argues that habit and long familiarity give old friendships a weight that new ones do not have.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar asks what long familiarity is worth, and Cicero answers that its worth lies in the ease that habit brings.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 19 (§68), trans. E. S. Shuckburgh
philosophy._accuracy_note: Values familiarity in general but does not speak to owning a friend’s acts.

kurals.tamil:
விழைதகையான் வேண்டி இருப்பர் கெழுதகையாற்
கேளாது நட்டார் செயின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vizhaidhakaiyaan vendi iruppar kezhudhakaiyaar
kelaadhu nattaar seyin.
kurals.meaning: When friends, by right of their closeness, do something without asking, the wise welcome it as something they wanted, because it came from someone they love.
kurals.elementary: Your friend sees your bike tyre is flat and pumps it up while you are at lunch, without asking. You don’t say, ‘Who gave you permission?’ You say, ‘Thanks!’ That is how old friends treat each other.
kurals.university: The key phrase is kelaadhu (கேளாது, ‘without asking’): the friend acts for us kezhudhakaiyaal, ‘by the right of intimacy’. The wise respond vizhaidhakaiyaan (விழைதகையான், ‘because of its desirability’), and vendi iruppar, ‘remain as those who wanted it’. Mu. Varadarasanar emphasises honouring the right itself, while Solomon Pappaiah says the wise accept the act even when they already knew of it, because it was done willingly by a friend. Kalaignar and Puliyur Kesigan make the same point more plainly: a good friend accepts what was done unasked. The couplet assumes a household culture in which a close friend may lawfully use or dispose of what is ours. Both base texts agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Sudama leaves Krishna’s palace without having asked for anything. When he gets home, he finds that Krishna has already, without a word, turned his hut into a mansion and ended his poverty, and Sudama accepts the gift with humility and gratitude.
hinduism.explanation: In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna acts for his old friend without being asked, and the friend receives it as an act of love, not an intrusion.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s situation: a friend acts unasked out of intimacy, and the other welcomes it.

christianity.quote_or_event: In a parable, Jesus describes a man who goes to his friend at midnight and asks to borrow three loaves for an unexpected guest, sure that friendship gives him the right to ask even at that hour.
christianity.explanation: The parable assumes that a friend may make demands that would be unthinkable from a stranger.
christianity.tie_back: It reflects the same culture of intimate claims the Kural assumes, though here the friend asks and is grudgingly answered.
christianity._accuracy_note: Weak match: the parable is about persistence in prayer, and the friend responds reluctantly.

islam.quote_or_event: “or [from houses] whose keys you possess or [from the house] of your friend. There is no blame upon you whether you eat together or separately.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an lists a friend’s house among the places where a believer may eat without blame, alongside the homes of close relatives.
islam.tie_back: This makes into law the liberty the Kural describes: a close friend may take from what is ours without a formal request.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on licensed familiarity between friends; the verse sets out a permission rather than praising the host’s welcome.

judaism.quote_or_event: Years after Jonathan’s death, King David asks whether anyone of Saul’s house is left to whom he can show kindness for Jonathan’s sake. He brings Jonathan’s lame son Mephibosheth to his table for life and restores Saul’s lands to him, though no one had asked him to.
judaism.explanation: David acts unprompted on the strength of an old friendship.
judaism.tie_back: This is friendship acting without being asked; Mephibosheth’s humble acceptance mirrors the welcome the Kural expects.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good fit for unasked kindness from an old bond; the stress is on the giver, not on how the recipient accepts it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The monastic code allows a monk to take an item ‘on trust’ (vissāsa) from a friend when five conditions are met: they are acquainted, intimate, the friend has spoken of it, the friend is alive, and the monk knows the friend will be pleased when the item is taken.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist monastic law recognises that among intimates, taking without asking is not theft if the friend would be pleased.
buddhism.tie_back: It is almost the Kural’s exact situation: an act done unasked by right of intimacy, and accepted because the friend wanted it.
buddhism.source: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga VIII (rule on taking on trust)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close in substance; the exact section was not re-verified live, so it is paraphrased.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pirithous raids Theseus’ cattle to test his famous strength. When the two men meet, each is so taken with the other that Pirithous offers to pay whatever penalty Theseus names, and Theseus instead forgives the raid and offers friendship.
greek_mythology.explanation: As Plutarch tells it, a liberty taken without leave becomes the start of a lifelong friendship rather than a quarrel.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Theseus welcomes an unasked act instead of resenting it, as the Kural advises, though here the friendship begins rather than having aged.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak match: the liberty comes before the friendship, not out of it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “it is fitting to go unasked and readily to the aid of those in adversity (for it is characteristic of a friend to render services, and especially to those who are in need and have not demanded them; such action is nobler and pleasanter for both persons)”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle praises the friend who helps without being asked, and says such help is more pleasant for both sides.
philosophy.tie_back: He shares Valluvar’s view that friendship works best through unasked acts that both sides welcome.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.11 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the value of unasked acts; Aristotle focuses on help in adversity rather than general liberties.

kurals.tamil:
பேதைமை ஒன்றோ பெருங்கிழமை என்றுணர்க
நோதக்க நட்டார் செயின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pedhaimai ondro perungizhamai endrunarka
nodhakka nattaar seyin.
kurals.meaning: If a friend does something that hurts you, put it down either to simple ignorance or to the great closeness that made them feel free to do it.
kurals.elementary: If your best friend borrows your favourite book and spills juice on it, think: ‘Maybe they didn’t know it mattered so much, or maybe they just felt at home with my things.’ Don’t decide straight away that they meant to hurt you.
kurals.university: Pedhaimai (பேதைமை, ‘ignorance, folly’) and perungizhamai (பெருங்கிழமை, ‘great intimacy, strong right of friendship’) are the two charitable explanations the couplet offers for an act that is nodhakka (நோதக்க, ‘fit to cause pain’). The particle ondro (ஒன்றோ) divides the commentators. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as ‘either … or’: ignorance or intimacy. Solomon Pappaiah reads ‘not ignorance only, but also great intimacy’. Puliyur Kesigan reads it as rejecting ignorance altogether: think of it as intimacy, not ignorance. The pairing is close to Arjuna’s pramādāt praṇayena vā (‘through carelessness or through affection’) in Bhagavad Gita 11.41, a parallel worth noting even though no direct influence can be shown. The text is the same in both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “I was ignorant of Your majesty, showing negligence and undue affection.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna explains his past familiarity with Krishna by two causes: pramāda (negligence) and praṇaya (affection).
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita offers the same two explanations as the Kural, pedhaimai and perungizhamai: an offence comes either from not knowing or from too much closeness.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 11.41 (trans. Swami Mukundananda; Sanskrit pramādāt praṇayena vāpi)
hinduism._accuracy_note: A notably exact parallel in its two-part diagnosis; the Gita is a confession by the offender, while the Kural advises the offended.

christianity.quote_or_event: From the cross, Jesus prays for those crucifying him, asking the Father to forgive them because they do not know what they are doing.
christianity.explanation: Jesus treats even a grave wrong as coming from ignorance and asks for pardon on that ground.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s first explanation, pedhaimai, ignorance becomes the reason for charity.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘they did not know’ reasoning, but concerns enemies, not old friends.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet warned believers against suspicion, calling it the most untruthful kind of talk, and told them not to spy on one another.
islam.explanation: Hadith literature urges believers to think well of one another (husn al-zann) instead of assuming bad intent.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise tells us to assume harmless causes when a friend’s act stings.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Good Manners (Adab), hadith on suspicion
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the charitable reading of others; paraphrased without a re-verified hadith number.

judaism.quote_or_event: “appoint for thyself a teacher, and acquire for thyself a companion and judge all men with the scale weighted in his favor.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah teaches dan le-khaf zekhut: judging others favourably by tipping the scale toward innocence.
judaism.tie_back: Reading a hurtful act as ignorance or intimacy is this favourable judgement applied to a friend.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:6 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on charitable judgement; it is not specific to old friends.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada advises attending to one’s own deeds, done and undone, rather than to the faults of others and what they have or have not done.
buddhism.explanation: The verse moves attention away from cataloguing others’ wrongs.
buddhism.tie_back: Declining to dwell on a friend’s offence is the habit of mind the Kural recommends.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Related only generally: it concerns self-examination, not interpreting a friend’s act.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles lets Patroclus fight in his armour but warns him only to drive the Trojans from the ships. Carried away, Patroclus pursues them to the walls of Troy and is killed, bringing Achilles terrible grief, yet Achilles never blames him and mourns him above everyone.
greek_mythology.explanation: The disobedience that cost Achilles his dearest friend came from eagerness and loyalty, not malice.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles reads his friend’s fatal act as zeal, not betrayal, much as the Kural asks.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrative; the Iliad does not frame Achilles’ response as a moral teaching.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus advises that when someone treats you badly or speaks ill of you, you should remember that they act from what seems right to them, and that they, not you, bear the harm of their mistaken view.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic method is to explain another’s wrong by their own mistaken judgement, which takes the sting out of personal offence.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s first explanation, pedhaimai, turned into a mental discipline.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on attributing offence to the other’s ignorance; it does not include the ‘great intimacy’ explanation.

kurals.tamil:
எல்லைக்கண் நின்றார் துறவார் தொலைவிடத்தும்
தொல்லைக்கண் நின்றார் தொடர்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ellaikkan nindraar thuravaar tholaividaththum
thollaikkan nindraar thodarpu.
kurals.meaning: Those who keep within the true bounds of friendship will not give up their bond with long-standing friends, even when that bond brings them loss.
kurals.elementary: Suppose your oldest friend accidentally makes your team lose the big game. A true friend doesn’t say, ‘We’re done.’ They say, ‘We’ve been friends forever, and one bad game won’t change that.’
kurals.university: The couplet balances ellai (எல்லை, ‘limit, boundary’) against tholl-ai (தொல்லை, ‘antiquity’): ellaikkan nindraar are those who stand within the limit (of friendship’s ethic), and thollaikkan nindraar are those who have stood with us from long ago. Tholaividaththum (தொலைவிடத்தும்) is read by most commentators as ‘even in loss or ruin’, from tholai- ‘to be destroyed’. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all take it as ‘even when the old friend’s acts bring harm’. Puliyur Kesigan reads it spatially, ‘even when they have gone to distant places’, and also takes thollai in its modern sense of ‘trouble’, giving ‘those who stood by us in our troubles’. The two readings change the image but keep the ethic of not abandoning old friends. Both base sources give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Before the war, Krishna tells Karna that he is Kunti’s eldest son and could be king of the Pandavas. Karna refuses: Duryodhana gave him honour and friendship when others mocked his birth, and he will not desert him now, even knowing the Kaurava side will lose.
hinduism.explanation: In the Udyoga Parva, Karna chooses an old friend’s cause over a throne, knowing it will cost him his life.
hinduism.tie_back: He embodies the Kural’s ‘those who will not give up long-standing ties even in ruin’.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Karna’s reply to Krishna), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong fit, although Karna’s loyalty is to a friend whose cause is unjust, a tension the Kural does not address.

christianity.quote_or_event: Paul blesses the household of Onesiphorus, who often refreshed him, was not ashamed of his chains, and searched Rome diligently until he found him, while others in Asia turned away.
christianity.explanation: Onesiphorus stayed loyal when association with the imprisoned Paul was costly.
christianity.tie_back: He kept the bond when others broke it, as the Kural’s friend keeps faith in loss.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good fit for loyalty in adversity; the Kural also covers loss caused by the friend himself.

islam.quote_or_event: During the flight from Mecca, Abu Bakr hid with the Prophet in the cave of Thawr while their enemies searched for them; the Qur’an remembers him as ‘the second of the two’ to whom the Prophet said not to grieve, for God was with them.
islam.explanation: Abu Bakr stayed with his long-time companion at the moment of greatest danger.
islam.tie_back: His steadfastness is the Kural’s refusal to give up an old bond when it brings peril.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong example of loyalty under danger; the Kural’s case of harm caused by the friend is not covered.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thine own friend, and thy father's friend, forsake not; neither go into thy brother's house in the day of thy calamity: for better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs urges loyalty to one’s own friends and to friends inherited from one’s father, even above distant kin.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Forsake not’ is the Kural’s thuravaar (‘they will not give up’) applied to old, even inherited, friendships.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close in spirit; the Kural adds ‘even when the friend causes loss’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When misfortunes strike, he doesn't abandon you. When you're down & out, he doesn't look down on you.”
buddhism.explanation: Two of the seven marks of a friend worth keeping are loyalty in misfortune and respect in decline.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s friend who does not let go even in loss.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.35, Mitta Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match on not abandoning friends in hardship.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Through twenty years of Odysseus’ absence, the swineherd Eumaeus keeps faith with his master, refuses to serve the suitors’ interests, and welcomes the disguised stranger kindly, at cost and risk to himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: Eumaeus’ loyalty to an old bond holds up through loss, hardship and pressure from those in power.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is the Kural’s ‘one who stands within the bounds’ and does not give up an old tie.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Loyalty of servant to master rather than between equal friends.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Surely he should keep a remembrance of their former intimacy, and as we think we ought to oblige friends rather than strangers, so to those who have been our friends we ought to make some allowance for our former friendship, when the breach has not been due to excess of wickedness.”
philosophy.explanation: Even where a friendship can no longer continue, Aristotle says past intimacy still creates obligations.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like Valluvar, holds that old friendship keeps its claim even after the friend has changed.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Aristotle allows a breach in some cases, while the Kural’s ideal never gives the friend up.

kurals.tamil:
அழிவந்த செய்யினும் அன்பறார் அன்பின்
வழிவந்த கேண்மை யவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Azhivandha seyyinum anbaraar anbin
vazhivandha kenmai yavar.
kurals.meaning: Those whose friendship has come down a long road of love do not stop loving, even when their friends do things that bring them ruin.
kurals.elementary: Think of a very old tree with deep roots. A storm can break some branches, but the tree is still standing the next day. A friendship that has grown for years is like that: even a big hurt doesn’t pull it out of the ground.
kurals.university: Azhivandha (அழிவந்த) are ‘things that bring destruction’, and the concessive seyyinum (‘even if they do’) leads to anbaraar (அன்பறார், ‘they do not cut off love’). The subject is anbin vazhivandha kenmaiyavar, ‘those whose kenmai (கேண்மை, friendship) has come along the way of love’, which commentators take as long-standing, inherited affection. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as friendship come down ‘from of old’ (தொன்றுதொட்டு), and Solomon Pappaiah as long-standing friendship. Puliyur Kesigan alone shifts the subject, reading it as ‘our love for them will not be cut off’. The couplet is the strongest statement of the chapter’s ideal and has been criticised by modern readers as possibly encouraging tolerance of harm; the traditional commentators keep it within the framework of a tested, virtuous friendship (compare chapter 80). The text is identical in both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After Rama helps him win back his kingdom, Sugriva forgets his promise to search for Sita while he enjoys his restored court. Rama is angered and sends Lakshmana to warn him, but when Sugriva repents, Rama receives him back and the alliance holds.
hinduism.explanation: In the Kishkindha Kanda, a friend’s neglect threatens Rama’s whole cause, yet Rama does not abandon the friendship.
hinduism.tie_back: Rama keeps his affection despite an act that threatened ruin, though his initial anger is greater than the Kural’s ideal allows.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Partial fit: the friendship survives, but only after a stern rebuke, and it is a new alliance rather than an old friendship.

christianity.quote_or_event: Peter, one of Jesus’ closest companions, denies him three times on the night of his arrest. After the resurrection, Jesus asks Peter three times whether he loves him and entrusts him with feeding his sheep.
christianity.explanation: The betrayal is answered with restored intimacy and trust, not rejection.
christianity.tie_back: Jesus’ love for Peter does not end even after the deepest failure, the Kural’s anbaraar in Gospel form.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong parallel of love surviving a friend’s betrayal.

islam.quote_or_event: “And let not those of virtue among you and wealth swear not to give [aid] to their relatives and the needy and the emigrants for the cause of Allāh, and let them pardon and overlook. Would you not like that Allāh should forgive you?”
islam.explanation: Classical commentators link this verse to Abu Bakr, who had vowed to stop supporting his relative Mistah after Mistah joined in slandering Aisha. After the verse came down, Abu Bakr resumed the support.
islam.tie_back: A long-standing bond survives a grievous injury, which is what the Kural asks of those whose friendship comes down the path of love.
islam.source: Qur’an 24:22 (Sahih International); occasion of revelation per Ibn Kathir
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match; the bond is kinship and patronage rather than friendship in the strict sense.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Saul rages at Jonathan that as long as David lives Jonathan will never be king, Jonathan still defends David, warns him, and renews their covenant, giving up his own claim to the throne.
judaism.explanation: Jonathan’s loyalty to David costs him his inheritance and his father’s favour.
judaism.tie_back: His love continues even though the friendship ruins his prospects, as the Kural describes.
judaism._accuracy_note: The loss comes from circumstance rather than from any wrong David did.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Devadatta, the Buddha’s cousin and an early follower, tries to split the Sangha and to have the Buddha killed. The Buddha meets him without hatred, and later tradition says Devadatta will himself eventually attain awakening.
buddhism.explanation: Even repeated attempts at destruction by a kinsman and former companion do not turn the Buddha to enmity.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the outer limit of the Kural’s ideal: love not cut off despite ruinous acts.
buddhism.source: Vinaya Pitaka, Cullavagga VII; later commentarial tradition
buddhism._accuracy_note: The Buddha’s freedom from hatred is not the same as continuing an intimate friendship.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Theseus joins Pirithous on his reckless plan to carry off Persephone from the underworld, though he knows it is folly, and both are trapped on enchanted seats in Hades until Heracles frees Theseus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Theseus stays loyal to his friend’s ruinous plan and pays for it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He keeps the bond even when the friend leads him to ruin, a vivid if cautionary version of the Kural.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrative only; the myth is often read as a warning against blind loyalty, not praise of it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If they are capable of being reformed one should rather come to the assistance of their character or their property, inasmuch as this is better and more characteristic of friendship.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says that when a friend goes wrong, the friendly response is to help him recover rather than to break off at once.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar he favours keeping faith with an erring friend, though he allows a break with the incurable.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Partial: Aristotle sets conditions on continued love that the Kural does not.

kurals.tamil:
கேளிழுக்கம் கேளாக் கெழுதகைமை வல்லார்க்கு
நாளிழுக்கம் நட்டார் செயின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kelizhukkam kelaak kezhudhakaimai vallaarkku
naalizhukkam nattaar seyin.
kurals.meaning: For someone so secure in an intimate friendship that they won’t even listen to others talking about their friend’s faults, the day that friend actually does wrong is a day of gain, because it proves their trust.
kurals.elementary: Someone at school whispers, ‘Your best friend said something mean about you.’ You say, ‘I don’t believe it.’ Later your friend really does make a mistake, and you work it out together. Your trust was strong enough to survive both the gossip and the mistake.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on repeated sounds: kel (கேள், ‘friend, kin’) + izhukkam (இழுக்கம், ‘fault’) is ‘a friend’s fault’, and kelaa (கேளா) is ‘not listening’. Its subject is the person vallaar (வல்லார், ‘skilled, strong’) in kezhudhakaimai who refuses to hear of a friend’s faults. The difficulty is naalizhukkam (நாளிழுக்கம்). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah, following the older interpretation, take the day the friend errs as a fruitful or useful day (பயனுள்ள நாள்) for such a person. Kalaignar reverses it: if friends wrong someone of such trust, all the days of that friendship are wasted. Puliyur Kesigan reads it as the friend’s fault seeming to be merely the fault of the day. G. U. Pope (‘The day his friend offends will day of grace to him appear’) follows the first reading. The text is the same in both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Bharata arrives at Chitrakuta with an army, Lakshmana suspects he has come to kill Rama and secure the throne, and urges Rama to fight. Rama refuses to believe ill of his brother and rebukes Lakshmana, and Bharata comes in fact to beg Rama to return.
hinduism.explanation: In the Ayodhya Kanda, Rama will not listen to a suspicion against someone bound to him by long love.
hinduism.tie_back: He shows the Kural’s kelizhukkam kelaa: refusing to hear accusations against an intimate.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Bharata’s arrival at Chitrakuta)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of refusing tales against an intimate, though between brothers rather than friends.

christianity.quote_or_event: Paul writes that love thinks no evil, bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things and endures all things, and Peter adds that love covers a multitude of sins.
christianity.explanation: The New Testament describes love as slow to suspect and quick to cover a fault.
christianity.tie_back: This is the posture of the Kural’s friend, who will not hear accusations and takes a real fault calmly.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good thematic fit; paraphrased because the exact wording was not re-checked live this session.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an tells believers that if an untrustworthy person brings them news, they should verify it, lest they harm people in ignorance and come to regret what they did.
islam.explanation: Reports against others are not to be acted on until verified.
islam.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s refusal to take on trust others’ stories about a friend’s faults.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the caution about tale-bearers; the Kural goes further, refusing to listen at all.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the person who covers an offence for love’s sake with the one who keeps repeating it and so divides close friends.
judaism.tie_back: Refusing to repeat or hear of a friend’s fault keeps the friendship, as the Kural teaches.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close match on covering faults and resisting tale-bearing between friends.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Describing right speech, the Buddha says the disciple does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here in order to divide people, but reconciles those who are divided and encourages those who are united.
buddhism.explanation: Divisive tale-bearing (pisuna vaca) is listed among the kinds of wrong speech.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural approaches the same evil from the listener’s side, by refusing to hear the tale.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Addresses the speaker rather than the listener; related but not identical.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the legend of Damon and Pythias (Phintias), Pythias is condemned by the tyrant Dionysius of Syracuse, and Damon stands surety for his life. When others mock him for trusting that Pythias will return, Damon refuses to doubt his friend, and Pythias does come back in time.
greek_mythology.explanation: Damon will not listen to the scorn and suspicion of others about his friend’s faithfulness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His trust is the Kural’s refusal to hear of a friend’s faults.
greek_mythology.source: Legend of Damon and Pythias, reported by Cicero and Valerius Maximus
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A Greek legend about Pythagoreans rather than myth proper; the friend in the story never does err.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch’s essay on telling a flatterer from a friend warns that flatterers often try to slander a man’s true friends to him, and that a wise person guards against such whispering.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch treats slander against one’s friends as a typical tactic of the false companion.
philosophy.tie_back: This is why the Kural praises the friend who will not even listen.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend (Moralia)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Weak match: the general theme is present, but the specific passage was not re-verified.

kurals.tamil:
கெடாஅ வழிவந்த கேண்மையார் கேண்மை
விடாஅர் விழையும் உலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kedaaa vazhivandha kenmaiyaar kenmai
vidaaar vizhaiyum ulagu.
kurals.meaning: The world loves those who never let go of friends whose friendship has come down unbroken through the years.
kurals.elementary: People trust the kid who has had the same best friend since kindergarten. If you stick with old friends, others think, ‘I would like a friend like that too.’
kurals.university: Kedaaa (கெடாஅ) and vidaaar (விடாஅர்) carry isai-nirai alapedai, a metrical lengthening that also adds emphasis: ‘never ruined’ and ‘never letting go’. Vazhivandha kenmaiyaar are ‘those whose friendship has come down along an unbroken path’. The main verb vizhaiyum ulagu, ‘the world desires or loves’, makes loyalty to old friends a source of public esteem. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read ‘the world praises’, while Puliyur Kesigan reads ‘everyone in the world will want such a person as a friend’. Solomon Pappaiah adds the qualification ‘even if the old friend does harm’, linking this couplet to 807. The text is the same in both base sources; the sandhi-split ytamizh form keeps the alapedai spellings.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Hitopadesha’s first book, Mitralabha, tells how a crow, a mouse, a tortoise and a deer become firm friends and rescue one another again and again from hunters and snares; their steadfastness is held up as the model of winning friends.
hinduism.explanation: The fable collection offers lasting friendship as practical wisdom that everyone admires.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says the world loves the faithful friend, and the Hitopadesha teaches that faithfulness as a model.
hinduism._accuracy_note: General praise of constant friendship; no direct statement that the world loves the loyal.

christianity.quote_or_event: Proverbs teaches that a friend loves at all times and that a brother is born for adversity.
christianity.explanation: Constant love in every season is presented as the mark of the true friend.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s unbroken friendship is this ‘love at all times’, and it wins admiration.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on constancy; the theme of public esteem is absent.

islam.quote_or_event: In a hadith qudsi, God asks on the Day of Resurrection where those are who loved one another for His glory, and promises to shade them on the day when there is no shade but His.
islam.explanation: Friendship kept for the sake of God is promised the highest honour.
islam.tie_back: The Kural promises the world’s love to the steadfast friend; the hadith promises divine honour.
islam.source: Sahih Muslim, Book of Virtue, Good Manners and Joining of Ties
islam._accuracy_note: Related by honour for enduring love; paraphrased without a re-verified hadith number.

judaism.quote_or_event: After the story of Honi the Circle-Drawer, who slept seventy years and woke to find no one who knew him, the Talmud records the saying ‘either companionship or death’ (o chavruta o mituta).
judaism.explanation: Life without one’s long-known companions is portrayed as not worth living.
judaism.tie_back: This shows how much is lost when old bonds are broken, and so why the Kural honours those who keep them.
judaism._accuracy_note: Emphasises the value of companionship, not the world’s esteem for loyalty.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells Sigala that a true friend is the same in happiness and in sorrow: he shares one’s troubles and is ready even to give up his life for one’s sake.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta portrays the loyal companion as someone to be cherished as a mother cherishes her child.
buddhism.tie_back: Cherishing the steadfast friend parallels the Kural’s ‘the world loves’ the loyal.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Parallel in praising constancy; the angle of public reputation is weaker.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Orestes and Pylades, companions from childhood who stand together through exile, matricide and danger in Tauris, became the proverbial pair of perfect friends for later Greek and Roman writers.
greek_mythology.explanation: Their unbroken loyalty earned them lasting fame as the model of friendship.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The world’s admiration of them is exactly the Kural’s vizhaiyum ulagu.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Iphigenia in Tauris; later classical reception
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good fit for fame earned through lifelong friendship.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And the proverb is a true one, "You must eat many a peck of salt with a man to be thorough friends with him."”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius quotes the proverb that only long shared life makes a complete friendship.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘friendship come down an unbroken path’ is a friendship of many pecks of salt.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 19 (§67), trans. E. S. Shuckburgh
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the value of long duration; it says nothing about public esteem.

kurals.tamil:
விழையார் விழையப் படுப பழையார்கண்
பண்பின் தலைப்பிரியா தார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vizhaiyaar vizhaiyap paduba pazhaiyaarkan
panbin thalaippiriyaa thaar.
kurals.meaning: Those who never fall away from their good feeling toward old friends, even when those friends err, are loved even by people who wish them ill.
kurals.elementary: There is a kid in class who is always loyal to friends, even when they mess up. Even the kids who don’t like them much have to admit, ‘Well, they’re a really good friend.’ Loyalty earns respect even from rivals.
kurals.university: Vizhaiyaar (விழையார், ‘those who do not wish one well’, i.e. enemies) becomes the agent of vizhaiyappaduba (‘are desired, loved’), a chiasmus: the unloving come to love. Pazhaiyaarkan (பழையார்கண்) is ‘toward old friends’, and panbin thalaippiriyaadhaar are ‘those who do not part from their disposition of goodwill’. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all supply ‘even though the friends do wrong’, carrying over the theme of 805-808. Puliyur Kesigan reads the reward as enemies wanting such a person as a friend. Closing the chapter with enemies’ esteem completes an arc from defining pazhaimai (801) to its social reward (809-810). Both base texts agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Before the battle at Kurukshetra, Yudhishthira lays down his weapons, walks across to the opposing army and bows to Bhishma, who is fighting for the Kauravas out of old loyalty to the Kuru throne. Bhishma blesses him, and both sides revere the old patriarch throughout the war.
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma’s steadfast loyalty to his old bonds wins the reverence of the side he is fighting against.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim that even those on the other side honour the one who does not depart from old ties.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva (Yudhishthira seeks blessings before battle), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good fit for adversaries’ esteem; Bhishma’s loyalty is to a vow and a throne rather than to an old friend.

christianity.quote_or_event: Paul urges believers, quoting Proverbs, that if an enemy hungers they should feed him, for by doing so they heap coals of fire on his head, and he tells them to overcome evil with good.
christianity.explanation: Steadfast goodness is presented as the way to change an enemy’s heart.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise expects goodness that does not waver to win over those who wish one ill.
christianity._accuracy_note: The mechanism, goodness winning enemies, matches; the specific virtue of loyalty to old friends does not.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon, the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that answering evil with good can turn an enemy into a devoted friend.
islam.tie_back: As the Kural says of the loyal friend, unwavering goodness makes those who wished ill come to love.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on enemies won over by goodness; the Kural’s particular virtue is loyalty to old friends.

judaism.quote_or_event: Avot de-Rabbi Natan asks who is the mightiest of the mighty and answers: one who makes his enemy into his friend.
judaism.explanation: The rabbinic text treats turning an enemy into a friend as the highest strength.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural describes the same transformation, enemies coming to love, as the reward of steadfast friendship.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches the outcome; paraphrased without live verification.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada teaches that hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world; it is appeased only by non-hatred, and this is an eternal law.
buddhism.explanation: Lasting goodwill, not retaliation, is what ends enmity.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s unwavering goodwill likewise wins over those who wish one ill.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches the overcoming of enmity; it is not specifically about old friendship.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On the battlefield at Troy, the Greek Diomedes and the Lycian Glaucus discover that their grandfathers were guest-friends. Though on opposite sides, they refuse to fight each other, exchange armour, and part as friends, honouring the ancient bond.
greek_mythology.explanation: An inherited friendship from earlier generations is respected even in the middle of war.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Loyalty to pazhaiyaar, old ties, turns enemies into friends, as the Kural’s last couplet says.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong fit: an old, inherited friendship honoured across enemy lines.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “They should, as I have been told that Cato used to say, rather be unstitched than torn in twain”
philosophy.explanation: Even when a friendship must end, Cicero advises letting it fade gently rather than breaking it violently, out of respect for what it was.
philosophy.tie_back: Both writers keep goodwill toward old friends; Cicero applies it to parting, Valluvar to never parting.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 21 (§76), trans. E. S. Shuckburgh
philosophy._accuracy_note: Weak match: it concerns how to end a friendship, which the Kural’s ideal does not consider, and says nothing of enemies’ esteem.
